89.title: One goal, as in Lens
89.standfirst: In 1998 France needed the World Cup's first golden goal to get past Paraguay. Twenty-eight years later, in Philadelphia heat, they needed a penalty — and little else changed.
prose: On the evening of the Fourth of July, in heat that slowed everything except the clock, France beat Paraguay 1-0 at Lincoln Financial Field. Kylian Mbappé converted a 70th-minute penalty — his 19th World Cup goal — and Les Bleus moved into a fourth consecutive quarter-final. For Paraguay, a first World Cup in sixteen years ended in the round of 16. For France, a tournament that had been all fluency finally asked for patience instead, and got it.

France and Paraguay had met at a World Cup only twice before, and both meetings sit oddly in the memory. In Sweden in 1958, France won 7-3, Just Fontaine scoring a hat-trick on the way to his thirteen goals, a record still unbroken. Forty years later, in Lens, the sides played 113 scoreless minutes — Zinedine Zidane suspended, José Luis Chilavert repelling everything — until Laurent Blanc turned in David Trezeguet's header in the 114th, the first golden goal ever scored at a World Cup. France went on to win that tournament. Didier Deschamps captained that side; on Saturday he watched from the touchline as the pattern repeated at a gentler tempo.

Paraguay had waited a long time for this stage. Absent since the 2010 quarter-final in South Africa, where eventual champions Spain edged them out, Gustavo Alfaro's side opened this tournament with a 1-4 defeat to the United States and then conceded twice in four matches. They beat Türkiye 1-0, drew with Australia, and in Boston held Germany to 1-1 before winning the shoot-out 4-3 — the first penalty shoot-out Germany have ever lost at a World Cup. Their goals came sparingly all summer: three in five matches, one each from Mauricio, Matías Galarza and Julio Enciso.

France have scored fourteen times in five games — 3-1 against Senegal, 3-0 against Iraq on this same Philadelphia pitch, 4-1 against Norway, 3-0 against Sweden, and now the one here — with the goals concentrated where you would expect: seven for Mbappé, four for Ousmane Dembélé, two for Bradley Barcola, one for Désiré Doué. Paraguay gave that attack its quietest night of the month. Gómez's back line sat deep, the heat did the rest, and for seventy minutes the game had the shape of Lens. Then came the penalty, and Mbappé, and a lead Paraguay had not scored enough all tournament to threaten.

So the tie closed two ledgers at once. Paraguay went home with the Germany shoot-out as the keepsake of a return sixteen years in the making, the 2010 quarter-final still their high-water mark. France moved on to a quarter-final of their own, a fourth in succession, every one of them reached under Deschamps — who said eighteen months ago that this tournament would be his last. The scoreline against Paraguay remains what it was in 1998: one goal, eventually, and no way back.
threads: Laurent Blanc's 114th-minute winner in Lens in 1998 was the first golden goal in World Cup history.
Mbappé's penalty was his 19th World Cup goal and his seventh of this tournament.
France have won all three World Cup meetings: 7-3 in 1958, 1-0 in 1998, 1-0 in 2026.
This was France's fourth consecutive quarter-final, all four under Deschamps, in his final tournament in charge.
89.meaning: Paraguay rebuilt the wall of Lens; France, once again, needed only one way through.

90.title: Same opponent, wider gap
90.standfirst: Morocco's 3-0 win in Houston ended the best World Cup a Canadian men's team has played and set up a quarter-final against France, a rematch of the 2022 semi-final. The only previous meeting between the two ended the same way: Morocco advancing, Canada going home.
prose: The co-hosts' World Cup ended at midday in Houston, a long way from home in more than one sense. Morocco's 3-0 win at NRG Stadium carried them into a second consecutive quarter-final and closed the deepest run a Canadian men's side has ever made. It also confirmed the cost of the Switzerland defeat in the final group game, which took away top spot and any knockout football on home soil; a tournament Canada part-owns finished, for them, in Los Angeles and then Texas.

These teams had met once before at a World Cup, and that afternoon decided things too. In Doha in December 2022, Hakim Ziyech capitalised on a defensive mistake inside four minutes, Youssef En-Nesyri added a second, and Nayef Aguerd's own goal gave Canada only consolation in a 2-1 defeat that sent Morocco through as group winners — their first knockout place in 36 years — and sent Canada home without a point. Morocco went on to a first African semi-final and fourth place. The distance between the two programmes has not narrowed since.

Morocco arrived in Houston unbeaten in this tournament, as they have been almost everywhere lately — BBC Sport put their run at 34 matches without defeat. They had drawn with Brazil, beaten Scotland and Haiti, and then held their nerve in Monterrey to put out the Netherlands on penalties. Canada's group stage contained the men's programme's first World Cup point and first win, a 6-0 dismantling of Qatar, and the 1-0 round-of-32 result against South Africa was a first knockout victory. Alphonso Davies, who tore an ACL on international duty in March 2025, was never fully himself here; the Guardian has since reported that the exit revived questions over how his recovery was managed.

For half the match Canada stayed in it. On 50 minutes Azzedine Ounahi put Morocco ahead, and the game found its level. Morocco's goals had been shared around this summer — Ismael Saibari with three, Achraf Hakimi and Soufiane Rahimi among the others — and here the load passed to Ounahi, the Girona midfielder who first announced himself at Qatar 2022. His second came on 82 minutes, his first two goals of the tournament arriving in a single afternoon, with Rahimi scoring the other. Jonathan David, Canada's leading scorer with three, was given nothing by the back line protecting Yassine Bounou, and Morocco recorded a second clean sheet of the tournament.

What the win opened for Morocco is the fixture the bracket had been holding back: France in Boston on 9 July, a rematch of the 2022 semi-final that France won 2-0. Across this World Cup and the last, Morocco have removed Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands and Canada from World Cup knockout rounds, and the question of whether they belong among the tournament's heaviest names is no longer seriously asked. For Canada, the accounting is quieter: a first point, a first win, a first knockout victory — and a hard reading of what the Davies episode cost, before Jesse Marsch's side decide what comes next.
threads: Azzedine Ounahi's goals on 50 and 82 minutes were his first two of the tournament.
Across 2022 and 2026, Morocco have removed Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands and Canada from World Cup knockout rounds.
Canada's first men's World Cup point, first win and first knockout victory all came at this tournament.
Morocco's quarter-final against France in Boston on 9 July is a rematch of the 2022 semi-final.
90.meaning: Canada found out how far they have come; Morocco showed them how far that still is.

91.title: The team Brazil never beat
91.standfirst: Norway reached the first World Cup quarter-final in their history by beating the one opponent they had never lost to — and Brazil, five-time champions, went out in the round of 16.
prose: Norway had never beaten Brazil, and they had never reached a World Cup quarter-final; on Sunday evening at MetLife they did both at once. Erling Haaland scored twice in the final eleven minutes to win it 2-1, and the five-time champions were out in the round of 16. It was the deepest Norway had ever gone, at only their fourth World Cup and their first in twenty-eight years.

The fixture had always carried one inconvenient line of history. Brazil had faced Norway four times — in 1988, 1997, 1998 and 2006 — and never won; now they had faced them a fifth, in a knockout tie, and lost again. The meeting that set the pattern was Marseille in June 1998, when Bebeto put the holders ahead with twelve minutes left, Tore André Flo equalised almost immediately, and Kjetil Rekdal's late penalty completed the turnaround — the night Norway first reached a World Cup knockout round. The reunion had been building all summer: Brazil's group this time contained both Morocco and Scotland, two of the other sides from 1998's Group A, and Morocco again took a point off them.

The game turned late. Norway thought they had led early through Patrick Berg, but the effort was clearly offside; Brazil then spurned the better chance of the first half when Bruno Guimarães' 14th-minute penalty, won after a challenge on Matheus Cunha, was saved by Ørjan Nyland. For an hour it stayed goalless. Then Haaland, quiet until that point, scored on 79 minutes and again on 90, his sixth and seventh goals of the tournament, and the tie was gone. Neymar converted a penalty deep into stoppage time, but it was only consolation.

Carlo Ancelotti's first tournament in charge of Brazil ended earlier than the reputation suggests it should. Norway, by contrast, had arrived carrying a forward in the form of his life: Haaland reached the last eight with braces against Iraq and Senegal, the 86th-minute winner over Côte d'Ivoire that gave Norway the first knockout win in their history, and now two more against Brazil — seven in five matches, from a player who came to the tournament with 55 international goals in 50 caps.

Both of Norway's previous last-16 visits, in 1938 and 1998, had ended in defeat to Italy; this time they went through, into a quarter-final against England, territory the country had never occupied. For Brazil, chasing a first title since 2002, it was the earliest kind of reckoning — and it left the old record intact, since a nation that has now met Brazil five times has still never lost to them.
threads: Norway have never lost to Brazil in five meetings: wins in Oslo 1997, Marseille 1998 and East Rutherford 2026, draws in 1988 and 2006.
Haaland scored his sixth and seventh goals of the tournament in the last eleven minutes; he arrived with 55 in 50 for Norway.
Bruno Guimarães had a 14th-minute penalty saved by Ørjan Nyland; Neymar converted one in stoppage time, too late to matter.
Norway's only previous last-16 trips, 1938 and 1998, both ended against Italy; this was their first quarter-final.
91.meaning: The five-time champions were the ones with something to disprove — and the record held: Norway have still never lost to them.

92.kicker: Round of 16 · Estadio Azteca · England 3-2 Mexico
92.title: Back to the Azteca
92.standfirst: England won at the Azteca for the first time since 1986, and did most of it a man short — two early Bellingham goals and a Kane penalty holding off the co-hosts after a red card.
prose: England won at the Estadio Azteca, which is not a sentence the ground's history had offered them before, and they did most of it a man short. Jude Bellingham scored twice inside three first-half minutes, Harry Kane's penalty proved the margin, and England came through 3-2 to reach the quarter-finals — their first competitive result on this pitch since June 1986, and a considerable improvement on the last one.

The setting had done the talking beforehand. England had not played a competitive match at the Azteca since 22 June 1986, the afternoon Diego Maradona scored twice in four minutes, once with his hand. Their only previous World Cup meeting with Mexico was the 1966 group stage at Wembley, won 2-0 through Bobby Charlton and Roger Hunt on the way to England's only title. The stadium — the only one to stage two World Cup finals, and now the first to host three tournaments — produced another England memory, of a different colour this time.

Bellingham settled it early, scoring on 36 and 38 minutes to put England two clear before Julián Quiñones pulled one back for Mexico on 42 minutes. The game turned on the 54th minute, when Jarell Quansah was sent off and left England to defend for more than half an hour a man down. Kane converted a penalty on the hour; Raúl Jiménez answered from the spot with twenty minutes left, and England held from there.

Mexico's had been the cleanest route in the tournament — four wins, four clean sheets, none conceded, Javier Aguirre's side unbeaten and at home. All of it ended in an afternoon of three England goals and two of their own that were not enough. Both of Mexico's World Cup knockout wins in almost a century have come at the Azteca, but a first quarter-final since 1986 was not to be added; Aguirre, at this stage for the third time as Mexico's coach, again went no further.

England, less tidy all month than Mexico, reached the last eight the way they had reached the last sixteen — narrowly, and by holding a lead under pressure. Kane's penalty took him to five goals for the tournament; Bellingham's brace, his first of the World Cup, came under the most that had been asked of England so far. Norway, and Erling Haaland, waited in the quarter-final.
threads: Bellingham scored on 36 and 38 minutes; Kane's 60th-minute penalty was the margin in a 3-2 win.
England played from the 54th minute with ten men after Jarell Quansah's red card.
It was England's first competitive match at the Estadio Azteca since Maradona's two goals in June 1986.
Mexico arrived unbeaten with four clean sheets; Aguirre's side again fell short of a first quarter-final since 1986.
92.meaning: The Azteca held the best of Mexico's World Cup past and the worst of England's; this time it added to England's collection.

93.title: Iberia in Texas
93.standfirst: Spain reached the quarter-finals without conceding, a substitute settling the Iberian derby in stoppage time — and Cristiano Ronaldo's World Cup career ended in Texas.
prose: The second World Cup knockout meeting of Spain and Portugal went the way of the first. In Cape Town in 2010 it was David Villa's single goal and a Spanish march to the title; at AT&T Stadium on Monday it was Mikel Merino's, scored in the first minute of stoppage time, and a place in the last eight. Spain won 1-0, extended a month without conceding, and sent Cristiano Ronaldo home from what was surely his final World Cup.

It was a cagey Iberian derby, low and careful, and Portugal paid for playing it that way. Merino, on as a substitute, followed up his own quickly taken free-kick to nip into the box and finish past Diogo Costa. Ronaldo, 41 and at a sixth World Cup, had been a passenger for much of the night; the goal ended his tournament, and in all likelihood his World Cup career, after a performance his side had approached too cautiously to survive.

The rivalry lives mostly in club football, but the international meetings have a habit of mattering. Portugal put Spain out of Euro 2004 at the group stage; Spain needed a semi-final shootout at Euro 2012; the sides shared six goals in Sochi in 2018, Ronaldo completing a hat-trick with an 88th-minute free kick. Only a year earlier, in June 2025, Portugal had taken the Nations League final in Munich on penalties after a 2-2 draw. The recent ledger had been even. This tie tilted it back to Spain.

Spain's tournament had been nearly silent at the back. After a goalless opening against Cabo Verde — the smallest nation ever to reach the knockout rounds — they beat Saudi Arabia, Uruguay and Austria, then Portugal, and had still not conceded a goal. They might have won this one earlier: Costa made a double save from Lamine Yamal and Álex Baena inside the first twenty minutes, and Mikel Oyarzabal, put through by Dani Olmo, dragged a clear chance wide with eight minutes left before Merino spared him.

There was a quiet symmetry in the dugouts, Portugal picked by Roberto Martínez, a Spaniard, and Spain by Luis de la Fuente, whose side had yet to concede to anyone. Champions in 2010 and pursuing a second title, Spain moved on to a quarter-final with Belgium. Portugal, whose best remains third place in 1966, went home having never reached a World Cup final — and, this time, without the player who had carried them to the edge of one.
threads: Spain reached the quarter-finals without conceding a goal all tournament; the 0-0 with Cabo Verde was the only match they did not win.
Merino's winner came in the first minute of stoppage time, following up his own quick free-kick.
Spain have won both World Cup knockout meetings with Portugal: 1-0 in Cape Town in 2010 and 1-0 in Dallas in 2026.
The defeat ended the World Cup career of Cristiano Ronaldo, 41, at his sixth tournament.
93.meaning: One peninsula, one place in the last eight — and the quieter side took it.

94.kicker: Round of 16 · Seattle · Belgium 4-1 United States
94.title: As old as the tournament
94.standfirst: A home World Cup ended for the United States at the round of 16, Belgium's four goals exposing a defence that had been holding until it wasn't.
prose: The United States' home World Cup ended at Lumen Field, at the same stage a home World Cup had ended for them once before. Belgium scored four, Charles De Ketelaere twice, and won 4-1 to reach the quarter-finals; the tournament the Americans had reached the last sixteen of, on their own soil, went on without them. In 1994 it had been Brazil, 1-0 at Stanford, in this same round. This time it was a heavier scoreline and a clearer gap.

De Ketelaere settled it early, scoring on nine minutes and again on 33, either side of Malik Tillman's equaliser — his second free-kick goal of the tournament. The United States conceded within a minute of drawing level, and the pattern held: American defenders were at fault for the early goals, and a Matt Freese error let Hans Vanaken in for a third early in the second half. Romelu Lukaku added the fourth in stoppage time. Christian Pulisic, hurt in a challenge on the hour, watched the end from the bench.

The fixture is as old as the tournament itself. When the countries first met, on 13 July 1930 at the Parque Central in Montevideo, it was the opening day of the first World Cup; the Americans won 3-0, reached the semi-finals, and that third-place finish is still their best. The second meeting needs less introduction — Salvador, 2014, this same round, Kevin De Bruyne and Lukaku scoring in extra time, Tim Howard making sixteen saves, the most recorded in a World Cup match since 1966. The third has now gone Belgium's way as well.

Rudi García's Belgium, rebuilt around the survivors of the golden generation, had spent the tournament trading goals — level with Egypt, goalless with Iran, five past New Zealand, then a 3-2 win over Senegal in the knockout opener. Against the United States they simply had more, and the win stretched an unbeaten run to eighteen matches. De Ketelaere, long spoken of and often doubted, delivered on the night it was most useful.

Mauricio Pochettino's side had reached the last sixteen with four past Paraguay, a win over Australia and a defeat by Türkiye behind them, and Folarin Balogun restored after a red-card suspension was lifted. It was not enough. A home World Cup went no further than one had gone before, and Belgium moved on to a quarter-final with Spain — evidence, for now, that what came after the golden generation is a team in its own right.
threads: De Ketelaere scored on 9 and 33 minutes and set up a third; Lukaku added the fourth in stoppage time.
The countries have now met three times at a World Cup — USA 3-0 in Montevideo in 1930, Belgium 2-1 in Salvador in 2014, Belgium 4-1 in Seattle in 2026.
The win extended Belgium's unbeaten run to eighteen matches.
The United States' home World Cup ended in the round of 16, as their 1994 home tournament had — that time to Brazil at Stanford.
94.meaning: Each side had come to prove its best World Cup was not already behind it; Belgium did, and sent the hosts home to ask the question of themselves.

95.title: Two eras cross in Atlanta
95.standfirst: Two down and eleven minutes from going out, the holders scored three times to beat Egypt — Messi the equaliser, Enzo Fernández the stoppage-time winner — in one of the tournament's great recoveries.
prose: Argentina's title defence was minutes from ending in Atlanta, and then it wasn't. Two goals down to Egypt in the 79th minute, the holders scored three times in the closing stretch — Cristian Romero heading in a lifeline, Lionel Messi levelling from close range on 83 minutes, Enzo Fernández heading the winner in the second minute of stoppage time — to win 3-2. It was the second round running that the champions had been dragged to the wire, and the second running they had come through.

Egypt had earned the scare. Yasser Ibrahim gave them a shock lead midway through the first half, Messi's penalty was saved, and Mostafa Zico put the Pharaohs two clear after the hour, an earlier effort of his having been ruled out by VAR. Hossam Hassan's side defended in the image they had held all tournament — chances rationed, the big moments taken — and for a quarter of an hour they were the team going through.

The two nations had never met at a World Cup, and had played only twice in ninety-eight years — a 6-0 Argentina win in the semi-final of the 1928 Olympic tournament in Amsterdam, and a 2-0 friendly in 2008 that Messi missed. The tie's billing had been the crossing it arranged: Messi, 39, against Mohamed Salah, 34, the two forwards who defined their countries, sharing a pitch for the only time. Salah captained Egypt through the fright; the finish, in the end, belonged to Messi.

For Egypt this was already a tournament without precedent. They had arrived having never won a World Cup match in three previous appearances, and left with two wins — the first, over New Zealand, coming ninety-two years after their debut — a group survived, and a first knockout tie since 1934 reached by beating Australia on penalties. Against the champions they went closer than anyone to ending the defence, and were beaten only in stoppage time.

Eight of Argentina's goals this tournament were Messi's, but the round of 16 was settled by the players around him — Romero's header, Fernández's winner — after Cabo Verde had taken them to extra time a round earlier. Scaloni's side stayed on course for the bicampeonato, a successful defence, and moved on to a quarter-final with Switzerland. Twice now they have looked like leaving early; twice they have found the late goal the occasion demanded.
threads: Argentina trailed 2-0 in the 79th minute and won 3-2, Enzo Fernández heading the winner in the second minute of stoppage time.
Messi's penalty was saved before he equalised from open play on 83 minutes — his eighth goal of the tournament.
It was the champions' second successive 3-2 knockout win from a difficult position, after Cabo Verde took them to extra time.
Egypt, without a World Cup win in three previous tournaments, went out having won two matches and pushed the holders to stoppage time.
95.meaning: Not a rivalry but an intersection — and the holders, for the second round running, needed the very end of it.

96.kicker: Round of 16 · Vancouver · Switzerland 0-0 Colombia (4-3 pens)
96.title: The quiet tie of the eight
96.standfirst: The quietest tie of the round produced no goals in 120 minutes and a shootout that Switzerland won, Gregor Kobel's save carrying them to a first quarter-final since 1954.
prose: The tie the previews skimmed ended the way its billing suggested it might — with no goals, and with the margins deciding it. Switzerland and Colombia played out 120 scoreless minutes at BC Place, and Switzerland won the shootout 4-3, Rubén Vargas scoring the last kick. It carried Murat Yakin's side to a quarter-final for the first time since 1954, when they were hosts — a stage reached before Colombia had played a World Cup at all.

The football offered little; the shootout offered the drama it had withheld. Gregor Kobel saved from Cucho Hernández and Davinson Sánchez struck the bar, and though Manuel Akanji fired over for Switzerland, the two Colombian misses were enough. Vargas held his nerve with the winning kick. Switzerland had not won a World Cup knockout tie since 1938; they ended the wait the only way this match was ever going to allow.

The sides had met at a World Cup exactly once, and the memory was a strange one. Stanford, June 1994: Hernán Gaviria and Harold Lozano scored, Colombia won 2-0, and a gifted side that had malfunctioned for two matches produced its best football too late — Colombia went home on three points, while a beaten Switzerland went through. This was their first meeting in a knockout round, and this time defeat was the better evening for no one.

Both had arrived unbeaten. Switzerland had taken the group from Canada with a win in Vancouver — the result that denied the co-hosts a home last-32 tie — and this was their third consecutive match at BC Place. Johan Manzambi, the 20-year-old Freiburg midfielder who scored twice against Bosnia, had been the find of their summer. Colombia had conceded once in four matches and kept three straight clean sheets for the first time in their World Cup history, Néstor Lorenzo's full-backs pushed high and James Rodríguez running the supply. Neither side could add to those numbers here.

Since 1994 the Swiss had reached the last 16 five times and lost every one; this was the sixth, and the first they survived. It took them to a quarter-final with the defending champions, Argentina, and to their own high-water mark — a stage Colombia have reached once, in 2014, and Switzerland had not touched in seventy-two years. The quietest tie of the eight had the most patient queue behind it, and Switzerland moved to the front of it.
threads: Goalless after 120 minutes; Switzerland won the shootout 4-3, Rubén Vargas scoring the decisive kick.
Gregor Kobel saved from Cucho Hernández and Davinson Sánchez hit the bar; Switzerland's only miss, by Akanji, did not cost them.
It was Switzerland's first World Cup knockout win since 1938 and their first quarter-final since they hosted in 1954.
The sides' only previous World Cup meeting, Stanford 1994, ended with Colombia winning 2-0 and going out while Switzerland advanced.
96.meaning: Two countries with the same old ceiling; on a night of no goals, Switzerland were the one that finally rose through it.

97.title: The Doha rematch
97.standfirst: Nearly four years after Al Khor, the same two teams met at the same stage, and France won by the same score — Mbappé and Dembélé settling the Doha rematch.
prose: The rematch produced the result it was echoing. France beat Morocco 2-0 in the quarter-final at Gillette Stadium, the identical scoreline to their 2022 semi-final in Qatar, and reached the last four again. Kylian Mbappé scored one and made the other, Ousmane Dembélé took the second, and Didier Deschamps' side moved to within a match of a third consecutive World Cup final.

It was not without a scare of its own making. Mbappé missed a first-half penalty, and for an hour the tie stayed goalless against a Morocco side that had specialised all tournament in staying in matches. Then Mbappé scored on 60 minutes — his 20th World Cup goal, one behind Messi's all-time twenty-one — and set up Dembélé six minutes later for the fifth of the Frenchman's tournament. France had held a commanding edge throughout, 21 shots on goal to four, and once the first went in the outcome was not in doubt.

Both sides knew exactly which rematch this was. In December 2022 they had met in the semi-final at Al Bayt Stadium in Al Khor, and France won 2-0: Théo Hernández volleying in inside five minutes, Randal Kolo Muani turning in a second late. France went to the final; Morocco went to the third-place match, the first African and first Arab nation to reach a World Cup semi-final. That night was the memory Morocco carried into this one, and the scoreline they were made to relive.

The roads here had read as inversions. France arrived without conceding in the knockouts — 3-0 against Sweden, 1-0 against Paraguay — the familiar shape of a Deschamps tournament, patience where it was needed. Morocco had ridden the fine margins, surviving the Netherlands on penalties after a 1-1 draw before a more straightforward 3-0 against Canada, Azzedine Ounahi scoring twice. Resilience had carried Walid Regragui's side to a second successive quarter-final; against France it met a side built to give nothing away, and gave nothing away again.

For Morocco the run ended one stage short of where it reached in Doha, though as expectation now rather than surprise. For France it continued in the only direction Deschamps' tournaments seem to travel — to a semi-final, in Dallas, against Spain or Belgium — and left them on track to become only the third nation to play in three consecutive World Cup finals. Deschamps has said this is his last tournament in charge; it is not finished yet.
threads: France won 2-0, the same score by which they beat Morocco in the 2022 World Cup semi-final.
Mbappé missed a first-half penalty, then scored his 20th World Cup goal and set up Dembélé's fifth of the tournament.
Morocco reached the quarter-final via a shootout win over the Netherlands and a 3-0 defeat of Canada; France had not conceded in the knockouts.
France advance to a semi-final against Spain or Belgium, on track to reach a third consecutive World Cup final.
Both managers remained from Doha: Didier Deschamps for France, Walid Regragui for Morocco.
97.meaning: The same two teams, the same stage, the same score — one carried what happened in Doha, and had to carry it again.

98.title: The debt of Puebla
98.standfirst: Forty years after Belgium ended a Spanish World Cup on penalties in Puebla, Spain answered — a second late Merino winner reaching the semi-finals, though their unbeaten knockout defence fell first.
prose: Forty years after Belgium ended a Spanish World Cup on penalties in Puebla, Spain answered. Mikel Merino, again a substitute and again late, followed his winner against Portugal with another — pouncing on a goalkeeping error two minutes from time to beat Belgium 2-1 in Los Angeles and reach the semi-finals. The tie that had closed in 1986 with a Belgian five from five reopened, and this time it was Spain who went through.

The afternoon turned on fine margins. Fabián Ruiz gave Spain the lead after half an hour, but Belgium — who lost Youri Tielemans to injury before kick-off and Thibaut Courtois to injury late on — drew level before the interval through Charles De Ketelaere, the first goal Spain had conceded in the knockout rounds. It stayed level into the closing minutes, until Courtois's replacement Senne Lammens could not hold a long-range effort from Pau Cubarsí and Merino was there to finish. The single decisive moment Spain had trusted all tournament arrived, for once, at the right end.

The fixture carried its own long memory. In Puebla in June 1986, Jan Ceulemans put Belgium ahead, Señor equalised with five minutes left, and 1-1 held through extra time before Belgium won the shoot-out 5-4, scoring all five, and went on to the semi-finals — the deepest run in their history. Four years later, in Verona, Spain answered with a 2-1 group win. Two World Cup meetings, one apiece; this was the third, and the one that finally repaid the older debt.

Luis de la Fuente's side, European champions two summers ago, had reached the last eight without conceding, winning by the smallest agreed margins — 3-0 against Austria, then 1-0 against Portugal, and now 2-1 here, the clean sheets interrupted but the results not. Merino's late winners in successive rounds have given a careful team its edge; the substitute has now scored the decisive goal in each of the last two.

For Belgium, rebuilt by Rudi García around the survivors of the golden generation, it was a familiar frustration — a lead surrendered, a match lost to a late goal, an eighteen-game unbeaten run ended one round short of the last four they reached in 1986 and 2018. For Spain, it is a first World Cup semi-final since they won the whole thing in 2010, and a meeting with France in Dallas. The shoot-out that once separated these teams was not needed; the football found a winner of its own.
threads: Merino's 88th-minute winner, after a Lammens error, was his second late knockout goal in a row, following the stoppage-time winner against Portugal — both off the bench.
De Ketelaere's equaliser was the first goal Spain conceded in the knockout rounds.
1986 quarter-final, Puebla: 1-1 after extra time, Belgium won the shoot-out 5-4; this was the sides' third World Cup meeting, and Spain's second win.
Belgium lost Tielemans to injury before kick-off and Courtois to injury late on; their unbeaten run ended at eighteen.
98.meaning: A tie that once needed penalties to separate them found a winner in open play — and the old debt was repaid.

99.title: The outsiders and the old habit
99.standfirst: Norway's run ended in extra time, Jude Bellingham scoring twice, and England reached a World Cup semi-final for the first time since 2018 — without the shoot-out their history feared.
prose: The outsiders were finally seen off, and it took extra time to do it. Jude Bellingham scored in the third minute of the added period to beat Norway 2-1 in Miami, his second of the match, and carried England into a World Cup semi-final for the first time since 2018. Norway's tournament — a first quarter-final, and the side that had removed Brazil — ended one round short of the last four.

Norway led it for a while. Andreas Schjelderup put them ahead on 36 minutes, and for the first time at this World Cup Erling Haaland was held without a goal, denied by Jordan Pickford at close range and later substituted in extra time. Bellingham equalised in first-half stoppage time and settled it early in the extra period. In between, Norway thought they had gone ahead when Torbjørn Heggem turned in a rebound just before the hour, but a review disallowed it for a foul by Haaland. The margins that had run Norway's way all tournament ran against them here.

The two nations had never met at a World Cup, and this first meeting reframed a familiar friendly rivalry — they first played in 1937, most recently a 1-0 England win at Wembley in 2014. England came in with the longer record and the heavier expectation; Norway with the momentum of a side that had already beaten Brazil and reached a stage the country had never occupied. For an hour it was Norway's game to lose, and they did not lose it cheaply.

England's World Cup past is bound up with the penalty shoot-out — four of them, only one won — and the 2006 quarter-final defeat to Portugal came at exactly this stage. This tie threatened the same shape, level and tightening, before Bellingham resolved it inside the first minutes of extra time and spared England the lottery their history dreads. Thomas Tuchel's team have not been imperious all month, but they have kept finding a way past sides that will not go quietly.

Bellingham's brace took him to six goals for the tournament, level with Harry Kane and behind only the eight of Mbappé and Messi; his two in the round of 16 against Mexico had come under pressure, and these came under more. England move on to a semi-final in Atlanta against Argentina — the reigning champions, and an old, heavy opponent. Norway go home having outgrown every expectation but the last one, the run ended by a country that has been here before and knows how it can go wrong.
threads: Bellingham scored in first-half stoppage time and again in the third minute of extra time; his brace took him to six for the tournament, level with Kane.
Haaland was held without a goal for the first time at the World Cup and was substituted in extra time; a Norway 'goal' on 56 minutes was disallowed for his foul in the build-up.
It was the first World Cup meeting between the nations; England reached a first semi-final since 2018.
England have contested four World Cup shoot-outs, winning one; this tie was settled in extra time instead.
99.meaning: One side had never been this far; the other had been here often enough to find the way through before the lottery arrived.

100.title: The narrow way through
100.standfirst: The holders needed extra time and a red card again, Julián Álvarez breaking a 1-1 deadlock in the 112th minute; Switzerland, down to ten, went out with their record against Argentina intact.
prose: Argentina found the narrow way through once more. The defending champions were level with Switzerland deep into extra time before Julián Álvarez struck from distance in the 112th minute, and Lautaro Martínez added a third in the closing seconds to make the 3-1 win look more comfortable than it was. It sent Argentina to a semi-final with England, and it followed the pattern of their whole knockout run: close, late, and survived.

Alexis Mac Allister headed Argentina ahead after ten minutes, turning in a Lionel Messi corner, but Switzerland were not the passive side the scoreline suggests. Dan Ndoye equalised on 67 minutes, and the game swung on a contested call moments later: Breel Embolo, already booked, was sent off after a video review overturned a yellow shown to Leandro Paredes — the second time the tournament has used the mistaken-identity protocol. Reduced to ten, Switzerland held out until Álvarez's strike, and then Martínez's, settled it.

The history belonged entirely to Argentina, and now stretches to three World Cup meetings, all won by them: 2-0 in the 1966 group stage, 1-0 through Ángel Di María's extra-time goal in the 2014 round of 16, and this. In eight meetings of any kind, Switzerland have still never beaten Argentina. The 2014 tie was the template — Switzerland holding on for almost two hours before a single late goal — and this quarter-final wore the same shape, down to the margin and the minute.

Lionel Scaloni's side have looked beatable throughout the knockouts and have not been beaten. Cabo Verde took them to extra time; Egypt led them 2-0 with eleven minutes left before a stoppage-time comeback; Switzerland took them to 112 minutes. Messi's run of scoring in nine consecutive World Cup matches ended here, but he made the opening goal, and the champions extended a World Cup unbeaten streak that now stands at twelve. The route has been a series of held breaths, each released just in time.

For Switzerland it was a first World Cup quarter-final since 1954, and the same old ceiling: they have never reached a semi-final, and left this one having pushed the holders as far as ten men could. For Argentina, England await in Atlanta — with the four highest-ranked teams in the world all now in the last four, the first time that has happened. The champions have learned to win the game that is still there to be won late; they have had to.
threads: Julián Álvarez broke a 1-1 deadlock in the 112th minute; Lautaro Martínez added a third in the last seconds of extra time.
Switzerland played the closing stretch a man down after Breel Embolo's second yellow, awarded when a review overturned a card shown to Paredes.
It was the sides' third World Cup meeting, all won by Argentina; Switzerland have never beaten them in eight meetings, nor ever reached a semi-final.
Messi's run of scoring in nine straight World Cup matches ended, but he assisted the opener; Argentina's unbeaten streak reached twelve.
100.meaning: A champion that has learned to win late met a side built to survive — and, for the third time at a World Cup, came out the right side.

101.title: Once before, in 2006
101.standfirst: France and Spain have met once at a World Cup, in 2006, and France won on their way to the final. Twenty years on they meet again in Dallas, the tournament's two form teams, for a place in the final.
prose: France and Spain arrive at the semi-final as the two teams the tournament has least troubled. France have not conceded in the knockout rounds — 3-0 against Sweden, 1-0 against Paraguay, 2-0 against Morocco — the settled shape of a Didier Deschamps side in what he has said is his last tournament in charge. Spain reached the last four without conceding either, until Belgium finally breached them in the quarter-final, and won anyway. In Dallas on Tuesday, one of the two loses for the first time when it matters, or does not lose at all.

They have met once at a World Cup, and it shaped a tournament. In 2006, in the round of 16 in Hanover, Spain led through a David Villa penalty before France won 3-1 — Franck Ribéry, Patrick Vieira and, last, Zinedine Zidane with a solo goal in stoppage time — on the way to a final France would reach and narrowly lose. It is the only time the neighbours have met at the finals, twenty years ago; most of the players who meet now were children when it happened.

Spain's month has been a study in economy. European champions two summers ago, Luis de la Fuente's side drew their opener with Cabo Verde and have won every match since, mostly by the smallest agreed margin — 1-0 past Portugal in an Iberian derby, 2-1 past Belgium — with Mikel Merino, a substitute, scoring the late winner in each of the last two rounds. Mikel Oyarzabal and Fabián Ruiz have carried the goals; Lamine Yamal, still a teenager, carries the expectation.

France have been the tournament's most fluent attack and one of its meanest defences at once. Kylian Mbappé shares the tournament's scoring lead on eight and has 20 World Cup goals, one behind Messi's all-time mark; Ousmane Dembélé, a hat-trick against Norway among his five, gives them a second edge. They beat Morocco 2-0 in the quarter-final, a rematch of the 2022 semi-final they also won, and have reached the last four without being seriously extended.

The stakes are large for both. France, runners-up in 2022, are one win from a third consecutive World Cup final — a place only two nations have ever reached; Spain, champions in 2010, are one win from a first final since. Deschamps is leaving; de la Fuente is building. Two European sides who share a border and, at the World Cup, almost no history are about to add the most consequential chapter to it.
threads: The sides have met once at a World Cup: France 3-1 Spain in the 2006 round of 16, Zidane scoring, on France's run to the final.
France have not conceded in the knockout rounds; Spain did not either until Belgium's goal in the quarter-final.
Merino has scored a late winner off the bench in each of Spain's last two knockout ties; Mbappé shares the tournament scoring lead on eight with Messi.
France are one win from a third straight World Cup final; Spain from their first since winning in 2010.
101.meaning: Two sides the tournament has barely touched, meeting for only the second time — with a final on the other side of it.

102.title: Not since 2002
102.standfirst: England and Argentina have met five times at World Cups, and not once since 2002. The rivalry — Maradona in 1986, the shoot-out in 1998 — resumes in Atlanta, with a final at stake.
prose: Of the four semi-finalists, these two carry the most history against each other and the longest wait to renew it. England and Argentina have met five times at a World Cup, home to some of the tournament's most replayed afternoons, but not once since 2002. In Atlanta on Wednesday the rivalry resumes with a place in the final on it — the reigning champions against the 1966 winners, back in the last four for the first time since 2018.

The ledger is long and uneven. England won the first meeting, 3-1 in the 1962 group stage, and the second, a bad-tempered 1-0 quarter-final at Wembley in 1966. Argentina answered in the 1986 quarter-final in Mexico City, where Diego Maradona scored twice in four minutes — the Hand of God, then the goal later voted the tournament's greatest — and won 2-1. In 1998 they met in the round of 16 in Saint-Étienne: 2-2 after David Beckham was sent off, Michael Owen scoring one of the World Cup's famous solo goals, before Argentina won the shoot-out 4-3. England had the last word in 2002, a Beckham penalty settling a group match 1-0. Five games, and not a dull one among them.

Argentina arrive as champions who have made the hard way a habit. Lionel Scaloni's side needed extra time to see off Cabo Verde, came from 2-0 down against Egypt in the final eleven minutes, and needed extra time again to beat Switzerland, Julián Álvarez settling it in the 112th minute. Lionel Messi, 39, has eight goals — level with Mbappé at the top — and the second title he is chasing would close the career the last one crowned. Their World Cup unbeaten run stands at twelve.

England have travelled more quietly and only slightly less anxiously. A well-drilled group stage gave way to knockout ties settled late — 2-1 against DR Congo, 3-2 against Mexico at the Azteca with ten men, and 2-1 against Norway in extra time, Jude Bellingham scoring twice. Harry Kane and Bellingham share the load with six goals each; Thomas Tuchel's side have not overwhelmed anyone, but they have not been put away. The shoot-out that shadows England's history — four contested, one won — has so far been avoided.

The prize is a place in the final at MetLife on 19 July. For Argentina it would be a second consecutive final and the chance to defend the title Messi won in 2022; for England, a first World Cup final since 1966, the year and the match that still frame every tournament they play. Two nations with a great deal of shared World Cup past, and none of it recent, meet again with the most at stake between them since the 1998 shoot-out in Saint-Étienne.
threads: England and Argentina have met five times at a World Cup — England won in 1962, 1966 and 2002; Argentina in 1986 and, on penalties, in 1998 — but not since 2002.
The 1986 quarter-final produced Maradona's two goals in four minutes; the 1998 round of 16 ended 2-2 before Argentina won the shoot-out after Beckham's red card.
Argentina reached the semi-final via extra time twice and a comeback from 2-0 down; Messi has eight goals, level with Mbappé.
England reached a first semi-final since 2018; Kane and Bellingham have six goals each, and England have avoided a shoot-out so far.
102.meaning: Five meetings, none in twenty-four years, and now the heaviest one yet — a final on the other side.

stars.name: Lionel MESSI
stars.line: 39 · FW · Inter Miami CF · 8 goals — hat-trick v Algeria, 2 v Austria, 1 v Jordan, opener v Cabo Verde; R16 v Egypt: the 83' equaliser in the 3-2 comeback
stars.why: The record is settled — twenty-one World Cup goals, more than anyone — and in the round of 16 the tournament asked what it was for. Argentina trailed Egypt 2-0 with eleven minutes left; Messi answered with the 83rd-minute equaliser that made the comeback possible before Enzo Fernández won it in stoppage time. At 39, at his sixth World Cup, the holders still turn to him when a match is slipping. It is habit now, not sentiment.

stars.name: Enzo FERNANDEZ
stars.tag: The header that saved the holders
stars.line: 25 · MF · Chelsea FC · his stoppage-time header beat Egypt 3-2 after Argentina had trailed 2-0 in the 79th minute · R32 3-2 aet v Cabo Verde
stars.why: Argentina's defence of the title has twice been taken to the edge, and in Atlanta it went past it: two goals down to Egypt with eleven minutes to play, one round after Cabo Verde had held them into extra time. Cristian Romero's header offered a lifeline, Messi levelled, and Fernández headed the winner in the second minute of added time to complete one of the great World Cup recoveries. The champions stayed on course for a successive title having, twice now, looked like leaving early.

stars.name: Kylian MBAPPE
stars.line: 27 · FW · Real Madrid · 8 goals — braces v Senegal, Iraq and Sweden, the 70' penalty v Paraguay, then the 60' opener that beat Morocco 2-0 in the quarter-final
stars.why: France have been the tournament's most fluent attacking side, and he remains its sharpest edge. In the quarter-final he missed a first-half penalty against Morocco, then scored the 60th-minute opener and set up Ousmane Dembélé for the second in a 2-0 win — a rematch of the 2022 semi-final settled by the same score. The goal was his 20th at World Cups, one behind Messi's all-time twenty-one, and left the two sharing this tournament's lead on eight. France go to a semi-final in Dallas; he no longer has to carry them, only to finish what they build.

stars.name: Ousmane DEMBELE
stars.tag: France's second scorer, and the clincher
stars.line: 29 · FW · Paris Saint-Germain · 5 goals — a hat-trick v Norway, one v Iraq, then the 66' second that beat Morocco 2-0 in the quarter-final
stars.why: France's attack has never leaned on one man alone, and Dembélé has been the proof: a hat-trick against Norway in the group stage, and, in the quarter-final, the goal that put the Morocco rematch beyond doubt, turning in Mbappé's pass six minutes after the opener. Five goals from the flank, in a side that keeps clean sheets at the other end. France, unbreached in the knockouts, go to a semi-final in Dallas.

stars.name: Yassine BOUNOU
stars.line: 35 · GK · Al Hilal · 90 caps before the tournament · Morocco: 1-1 Brazil, R32 1-1 v Netherlands (3-2 pens), R16 3-0 v Canada, QF 0-2 France
stars.why: The pattern held to the end. In 2022 he kept Spain scoreless for 120 minutes and saved two kicks in the shoot-out; this time the Netherlands were sent home from one, and against co-hosts Canada he kept a clean sheet as Morocco pulled clear. His tournament ended in the quarter-final against France, the 2022 rematch lost by the same 2-0 — a run that reached the last eight unbeaten before it met a side that had not conceded in the knockouts. Calm is a skill; his has aged well.

stars.name: Azzedine OUNAHI
stars.tag: The brace that beat the co-hosts
stars.line: 26 · MF · Girona FC · 2 goals — 50' and 82' in the 3-0 R16 win over Canada · Morocco unbeaten in five, the Netherlands beaten 3-2 on penalties
stars.why: Four years ago he was the unknown who left Spain's coach asking, mid-tournament, where he had come from. In the round of 16 he was the certainty: a goal either side of the hour against Canada, on 50 and 82 minutes, before Soufiane Rahimi added a third. Morocco went through the group stage and past the Netherlands unbeaten, and reached a second successive quarter-final — where France, the side that beat them in the 2022 semi-final, beat them again by the same 2-0. The debt carried four years from Doha was not settled.

stars.name: Mikel OYARZABAL
stars.line: 29 · FW · Real Sociedad · 2 goals in the 3-0 R32 win over Austria (36' and 89') · Spain: R16 1-0 v Portugal, QF 2-1 v Belgium
stars.why: The man who scored the goal that won Spain the last European Championship has been their most reliable finish here, twice beating Austria to end a fifteen-year wait for a World Cup knockout win. He might have had the Portugal tie too, spurning a clear chance late before Mikel Merino settled it. Spain reached the semi-finals having conceded just once in the knockouts — to Belgium, in a 2-1 quarter-final won by another late Merino goal. France, in Dallas, stand next.

stars.name: Mikel MERINO
stars.tag: A late winner in each knockout round
stars.line: 30 · MF · Arsenal FC · injury-time winner v Portugal (R16), then the 88' winner that beat Belgium 2-1 (QF) — both off the bench
stars.why: Spain have won the tight ones, and the same substitute keeps winning them. Merino came off the bench to score the stoppage-time winner against Portugal that ended Cristiano Ronaldo's World Cup, then did it again in the quarter-final, pouncing on a goalkeeping error two minutes from time to beat Belgium 2-1. Two late winners in two rounds, each from the bench, have carried Spain to a first World Cup semi-final since they won the tournament in 2010. France, in Dallas, are next.

stars.name: Charles DE KETELAERE
stars.line: 25 · FW · Atalanta BC · scored twice (9', 33') in Belgium's 4-1 R16 win over the United States, then the QF equaliser v Spain (41') · R32 3-2 aet v Senegal
stars.why: Belgium spent the round of 32 clinging on, beating Senegal only through a stoppage-time equaliser and a contested extra-time penalty. Against the co-hosts they were something else: De Ketelaere scored inside nine minutes, added a second before the half, and exposed the United States' defence in a 4-1 win. He scored again in the quarter-final, equalising against Spain — but a late Spanish goal beat Belgium 2-1 and ended their tournament, and an eighteen-match unbeaten run, in the last eight. The talent long spoken of arrived; the team around it fell just short.

stars.name: Erling HAALAND
stars.tag: The two goals that removed Brazil
stars.line: 25 · FW · Manchester City · 7 goals — 2 v Iraq, 2 v Senegal, 86' winner v Côte d'Ivoire (R32), then 79' and 90' to beat Brazil 2-1 (R16) · QF 1-2 v England
stars.why: Norway's first World Cup in 28 years, Haaland's first at all, and in the round of 16 it produced the upset of the tournament: two goals in the final eleven minutes against Brazil, after Ørjan Nyland had saved Bruno Guimarães' early penalty. The five-time winners went out; Norway reached a quarter-final for the first time in their history. In the last eight the tournament finally quieted him — held without a goal for the first time, and substituted in extra time as England won 2-1. Norway's deepest World Cup run ended one stage short of the semi-final, a long way beyond anything the country had reached before.

stars.name: Harry KANE
stars.tag: Past Pelé on World Cup goals
stars.line: 32 · FW · FC Bayern München · 6 goals — 2 v Croatia, 1 v Panama, 2 v DR Congo (R32), penalty v Mexico (R16)
stars.why: Kane's tournament has been quietly complete. His brace against DR Congo took him past Pelé's World Cup total; his 60th-minute penalty against Mexico kept England ahead in a 3-2 win they finished with ten men after Jarell Quansah's red card. At 32 he keeps arriving where matches are decided, the reliable half of an England attack in which Jude Bellingham has become the second, decisive scorer — it was Bellingham's brace that saw off Norway in the quarter-final while Kane went quiet. England, into a first semi-final since 2018, meet Argentina in Atlanta.

stars.name: Jude BELLINGHAM
stars.tag: Another brace, this one in extra time
stars.line: 23 · MF · Real Madrid · 6 goals — 1 v Croatia, 1 v Panama, 2 v Mexico (R16), then 2 v Norway (45'+2', 93') to win the QF in extra time
stars.why: England's second scorer has become their decisive one. After a brace against Mexico in the round of 16, Bellingham scored twice more against Norway in the quarter-final — an equaliser in first-half stoppage time and the winner in the third minute of extra time — to send England to a first semi-final since 2018. At 23 he now carries six goals, level with Harry Kane and behind only Mbappé and Messi, and a share of the load in the biggest matches England have played in years. Argentina, in Atlanta, are next.

stars.name: Gregor KOBEL
stars.tag: The save that sent Switzerland through
stars.line: 28 · GK · Borussia Dortmund · kept out Colombia through 120 goalless minutes, then saved in the shoot-out as Switzerland won 4-3 (R16) · QF 1-3 aet v Argentina
stars.why: Switzerland had not won a World Cup knockout match since 1938. In Vancouver they ended the wait the hard way: a goalless draw with Colombia across two hours, then a shoot-out Switzerland won 4-3, Kobel's save the difference, to reach a quarter-final for the first time in 72 years. The run ended there, in extra time against Argentina — still no semi-final in Switzerland's history, and still no win over the champions in eight meetings. A well-organised side found the margin that had eluded it at the last three tournaments, and then met the one it could not.

stars.name: Julián ALVAREZ
stars.tag: The strike that broke the deadlock
stars.line: 26 · FW · Atlético de Madrid · the 112' strike that broke a 1-1 deadlock against Switzerland; Argentina won the quarter-final 3-1 in extra time
stars.why: Argentina's knockout run has been a sequence of narrow escapes, and the quarter-final was the narrowest: level with ten-man Switzerland deep into extra time before Álvarez struck from distance in the 112th minute. It broke a game the champions had been unable to win in normal time, and sent them to a semi-final with England. Around Messi, Argentina have needed others to settle these matches — Enzo Fernández against Egypt, Álvarez here — and the title defence has stayed alive on the strength of them.
